transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-08
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes (recording had ~46:52 audio)
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dana Lee (CISO - Polaris), Marcus Reed (Head of Platform), Sana Patel (DevOps), Oliver Grant (Legal - joined ~25m)

Summary:
Quick security posture discovery to see fit for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer wants SOC2/ISO level assurance, SSO/SAML for non-interactive service accounts, RBAC & audit logs needs, KMS key control options and retention rules. Discussed trade-offs and next steps (send reports, schedule tech deep dive).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Alex Martinez, AE on the Redwood team. With me is Priya Shah, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Dana (Polaris - CISO): Good afternoon, thanks. I'm Dana, Polaris CISO. We wanted to have a quick overview of your security posture as we evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:13] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Dana. We'll go over SOC2, SSO, RBAC, audit logs, encryption/KMS and data retention. Happy to go deep on any of these.
[00:20] Marcus (Polaris): I'm Marcus, head of platform. We'll likely be the ones operating any dedicated or private deployment.
[00:25] Sana (DevOps): Hi, Sana here. We'll want to know throughput and how keys are managed, also what logs look like for compliance.
[00:31] Alex: Awesome. Quick qualification: are you leaning toward hosted for speed, or do you think you'll need dedicated/private for compliance?
[00:38] Dana: We're exploring. For some products, hosted could be fine if the controls line up, but for regulated flows we're leaning toward dedicated or private — especially because of KMS and audit requirements and data residency.
[00:48] Priya: Totally makes sense. For context, our hosted offering is SOC 2 Type II certified, we have encryption at rest and in transit, and we support bring-your-own-key via a KMS integration with our enterprise plan — there are some differences between hosted BYOK and full private where customer fully controls the network.
[00:59] Dana: Can you share the SOC2 report? And do you have ISO 27001?
[01:03] Alex: Yes, we'll send the SOC 2 Type II report and the pen test summary after this call. We don't currently have ISO 27001 certificate, we're evaluating it as part of our roadmap, targeted next year.
[01:12] Dana: Ok, that matters for executives. If you don't have ISO, we'll need to know compensating controls, audit cadence, vulnerability management.
[01:19] Priya: Understood. We have a mature vulnerability management program, quarterly internal scans and annual external pen tests, and we can share the details in the compliance pack.
[01:27] [01:30] Marcus: On SSO — our security org requires SAML-based SSO for both human users and non-human service accounts where possible. Do you support SAML for the console and API clients?
[01:38] Priya: For console and user logins we support SAML/SAML 2.0 with SCIM provisioning optionally. For API we recommend token-based service accounts; for enterprise customers we can integrate with your IdP to issue short-lived tokens via an OAuth flow. We can show a sample metadata file.
[01:50] Dana: So for API keys, you support rotating via KMS or are there long-lived keys? We need short TTLs, we can't have unlimited lifetime creds stored in plaintext.
[02:00] Priya: We don't store plaintext long-lived keys. On hosted BYOK you can have keys in your KMS and we encrypt model payloads at rest with those keys. API tokens are short-lived and can be issued by your IdP; we also have token introspection and revocation APIs.
[02:12] Sana: How do you handle RBAC? We need roles, least privilege, and audit trails per token.
[02:18] Priya: We ship RBAC in the console — roles like Admin, Developer, Read-only, and you can scope by project or route. All actions are logged to our audit log, which is available via the console and can be exported to your SIEM via streaming (Syslog / GCP Pub/Sub / AWS Kinesis).
[02:31] Dana: Audit logs retention is big for us — 7 years for some data. What's your retention policy and can we get an archive?
[02:38] Alex: By default we retain logs for 90 days in hosted, but we offer add-ons for longer retention, or we can stream logs to your own storage for long-term archival which you control. For dedicated/private, you control retention fully.
[02:52] Marcus: On encryption/KMS — if we go dedicated but hosted in your cloud, do we get BYOK with control over rotation? Or is it only for private?
[02:59] Priya: Dedicated gives you BYOK and rotation controls — you can provide a CMK in AWS KMS or equivalent in GCP, and we support rotation. With private deployment, keys never leave your environment. Hosted BYOK uses a trust boundary where you provide keys and we use them for at-rest encryption, but there are subtle differences in HSM-level guarantees. We'll put the exact matrix in a doc.
[03:18] Dana: Can auditors access the raw logs for e-discovery or is everything mediated through your console?
[03:24] Alex: Auditors can be given read-only access to logs if you choose, or we can set up a dedicated export of logs to your storage. We typically avoid handing over raw system-level access; instead we provide exports and signed attestations.
[03:36] [03:45] Sana: Network controls — we need VPC peering and dedicated subnets, plus private link access, can Redwood support that for the private offering?
[03:52] Priya: Yes, private deployments support VPC-only access, no public endpoints, and we support AWS PrivateLink and on-prem options. For Dedicated (reserved pools) we offer customer VPC peering in supported regions. We'll map region availability in the doc.
[04:08] Marcus: Latency trade-offs are important — if we push to private to meet compliance, what's the impact on throughput and cost?
[04:15] Priya: There's a cost/latency tradeoff. Private on-prem can have the lowest latency if you're colocated, but operational overhead rises. Dedicated hosted with reserved GPUs gives predictable throughput and similar SLAs to hosted but at higher cost. We'll provide a cost/throughput matrix for your expected token/sec in the follow-up.
[04:30] Dana: About data residency — we need to ensure EU data stays in EU for certain products. Do you support region pinning for hosted?
[04:37] Alex: Yes, hosted supports region pinning for enterprise customers, subject to model availability. Dedicated and private obviously let you choose region or on-prem. We'll need to confirm which models are available in those regions.
[04:47] Oliver (Legal, joined): Sorry I'm late. On the legal side, we need standard indemnities, and specific language about data processing, sub-processors, and breach notification times (48 hours). Is breach notification 48 hours standard?
[04:58] Alex: Our standard breach notification is 72 hours for the hosted offering; we can discuss tighter SLAs on enterprise contracts. We do use a sub-processor list and maintain an up-to-date registry. We'll include that in the pack.
[05:08] Dana: For discovery, can we do a 2-week pilot, maybe with token limits, to run sensitivity tests?
[05:13] Priya: Absolutely, we run pilots all the time — usually a dedicated small reserved pool or hosted with strict data handling rules. We'll scope pilot goals, throughput, and success criteria.
[05:20] Marcus: One technical ask: can Redwood's audit logs include request/response hashes or partial redaction? Some of our records are PII and cannot be stored in plaintext in logs.
[05:30] Priya: We support configurable redaction and hashing for request payloads in audit logs. For hosted, we have default redaction rules; for dedicated/private we can expose more granular controls and keep payloads out of logs entirely if required.
[05:43] Dana: OK, that's helpful. Also, do you support customer-managed HSM (like AWS CloudHSM) or only KMS?
[05:50] Priya: For private deployments, yes we can integrate with CloudHSM or on-prem HSMs. For hosted, we support KMS providers and HSM-backed KMS if the provider supports it; we can detail specifics per cloud.
[06:02] Alex: Quick note — we'll send the compliance pack with SOC2, pen test summary, sub-processor list, SSO/SAML guide, and the RBAC/audit export docs.
[06:09] [06:15] Oliver: We'll want to review the contract language around data processing. Expect our legal team to follow up with a redline.
[06:20] Alex: Totally. We'll loop in our legal.
[06:23] Marcus: Timing-wise we want a procurement timeline in July and potentially start pilot in late July / early Aug if approvals go through.
[06:31] Priya: We'll propose dates after we send the docs. Also, I'd recommend a technical deep dive with Marcus and Sana next week to map network/topology and sizing.
[06:40] Dana: Sounds good. Any surprises or edge cases we should know about?
[06:44] Priya: The main trade-offs are: hosted is fastest to get started but has limits on where keys live; dedicated gives better isolation and BYOK semantics; private gives the most control but needs more ops. We'll include specifics about rotation, key escrow (we don't keep backup keys for BYOK), and log export formats.
[06:58] Alex: Wrap up — recap next steps: Alex sends SOC2 & pen test; Priya sends SSO/SAML guide & RBAC/audit docs; schedule SE deep dive for private/dedicated; Polaris to confirm residency + pilot throughput.
[07:12] Dana: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[07:15] Alex: Thank you, we'll follow up via email with links and proposed times.

End of transcript.
